papers.title: Discovery of a Small-Molecule Modulator of the Autophagy Lysosome Pathway That Targets Lamin A/C and LAMP1, Induces Autophagic Flux, and Affects Lysosome Positioning in Neurons
papers.summary: This study reports the discovery of a small molecule that modulates the autophagy-lysosome pathway by targeting Lamin A/C and LAMP1 proteins. The compound was shown to induce autophagic flux and alter lysosome positioning specifically in neurons. This suggests a potential new tool for manipulating autophagic and lysosomal processes in neuronal cells.
papers.why: Since the PhD project focuses on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, this small-molecule modulator could serve as a valuable experimental tool for probing autophagy-lysosome dynamics in interneurons and related brain cell types.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Microautophagy: An Emerging Pathway in Maintaining Mitochondrial Homeostasis.
papers.summary: This paper reviews mitochondrial microautophagy, a lesser-studied pathway distinct from mitophagy in which small pieces of mitochondria are engulfed directly without full organelle degradation. It appears to be discussed as a mechanism cells use to fine-tune mitochondrial quality and quantity, complementing macroautophagy-based mitophagy. The abstract suggests this pathway is gaining recognition as important for overall mitochondrial homeostasis.
papers.why: Since the PhD project centers on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, understanding microautophagy as an alternative/complementary mitochondrial quality control pathway could refine interpretation of neuronal mitochondrial turnover, especially in metabolically distinct interneuron populations.

papers.title: Graph Neural Networks for Spatial Transcriptomics: A Review of Graph Design and Downstream Applications
papers.summary: This paper is a review of how graph neural networks (GNNs) are applied to spatial transcriptomics data, covering different ways to construct spatial graphs from tissue coordinates and gene expression. It surveys downstream tasks such as clustering, cell-type annotation, and spatial domain identification that these GNN models support. The review likely compares graph construction strategies and highlights strengths and limitations of various GNN architectures for spatial omics analysis.
papers.why: Since the PhD project integrates spatial transcriptomics with deep learning to study neuronal and interneuron organization, understanding GNN-based graph design choices could directly inform how spatial gene expression data around perineuronal nets and mitophagy-related genes are modeled and analyzed.

papers.title: Glucose and serum availability fine-tune neuronal metabolic adaptations and direct insulin signaling.
papers.summary: This paper likely explores how varying levels of glucose and serum in the cellular environment influence how neurons adjust their metabolism. It probably examines how these nutrient conditions affect insulin signaling pathways within neurons. The findings suggest that neuronal energy metabolism and insulin responsiveness are closely tied to the availability of external nutrients.
papers.why: Understanding how neuronal metabolic states and insulin signaling respond to nutrient availability could inform how mitophagy and autophagy pathways are regulated in neurons, particularly under varying metabolic conditions relevant to interneuron health.

papers.title: The Multimodal Pretraining Framework CarHE Predicts Spatial Transcriptomics in Tumors from Routine Pathology Images.
papers.summary: This paper introduces CarHE, a multimodal deep learning framework that pretrains on paired histology images and spatial transcriptomics data to predict gene expression patterns directly from routine pathology slides. It focuses on tumor tissue, aiming to bridge the gap between widely available H&E-stained images and costly spatial transcriptomics measurements. The framework demonstrates that spatial gene expression can be inferred computationally from standard pathology images, potentially reducing the need for expensive molecular profiling in some contexts.
papers.why: The multimodal pretraining approach linking histology images to spatial transcriptomics could inspire analogous AI strategies for inferring spatial gene expression or metabolomic patterns in brain tissue from routine neurohistology images, relevant to studying interneurons and perineuronal nets.
papers.figure: The figure showing the model architecture and workflow for aligning pathology image features with spatial transcriptomic gene expression predictions.

papers.title: Astrocytic LCN2 mediates pathological crosstalk with neurons to promote neuronal loss in sepsis-associated encephalopathy.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how astrocytes, a type of support cell in the brain, contribute to neuronal damage during sepsis-associated encephalopathy, a brain dysfunction linked to severe infection. The key mechanism involves a protein called LCN2, secreted by astrocytes, which appears to harm nearby neurons. This astrocyte-neuron pathological communication is proposed as a driver of neuronal loss in this condition.
papers.why: While focused on astrocyte-neuron signaling rather than mitophagy or interneurons directly, this work is relevant background for understanding non-cell-autonomous stress pathways that could intersect with neuronal autophagy/mitophagy dysfunction and vulnerability of specific neuronal populations in disease states.

papers.title: Glutathione Primes Mitochondrial Autophagy to Guide Pulp-Dentine Complex Repair.
papers.summary: This study investigates how glutathione, an antioxidant molecule, influences mitochondrial autophagy (mitophagy) in dental pulp cells. The researchers found that glutathione levels help trigger mitophagy, which in turn supports the repair process of the pulp-dentine complex after injury. This suggests a link between cellular redox state and the quality-control mechanisms that clear damaged mitochondria to promote tissue regeneration.
papers.why: Although focused on dental tissue rather than brain, this paper offers a mechanistic parallel for glutathione-mitophagy signaling that could inform how redox state regulates mitochondrial quality control in neurons.

papers.title: Heat shock-induced autophagy has cargo selectivity in <i>Saccharomyces cerevisiae</i>.
papers.summary: This paper studies autophagy in yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) triggered by heat shock, a form of stress. The researchers found that this stress-induced autophagy is not random, but selectively targets specific cellular cargo for degradation. This suggests that cells have specialized mechanisms to choose what gets broken down during heat stress, rather than just bulk degrading everything.
papers.why: Although this is a yeast study rather than neurons, understanding the molecular logic of cargo-selective autophagy under stress could inform how mitophagy and autophagy selectivity mechanisms operate in neurons, offering conceptual parallels for the PhD project's core biology.
